hops.title: Ask it: how does a frog get a drink?
hops.text: When the frog card turns up, ask, "A frog doesn't sip with its mouth. How do you think it drinks?" Expect great guesses, like licking puddles or gulping rain. Enjoy every one, then share the surprise: a frog soaks up water through a bare patch of skin on its belly and the undersides of its thighs.

sources.citation: Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture (University of Washington), "All About Frogs"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small green frog resting its belly flat on a wet mossy leaf beside a shallow puddle.
image.caption: A frog drinks through a patch of bare skin on its belly, not with its mouth.

hops.title: Say it: feathers and turtle shells are tough like your fingernails
hops.text: Try saying, "Tap your fingernail. Feel how hard it is? A bird's feathers and the hard plates on most turtle shells are made of tough stuff like that, too!" Use it while your child holds the craft feather or the turtle card. Their own fingertip becomes the link between a soft feather and a hard shell.

sources.citation: Arizona State University, Ask A Biologist, "Feathers"
U.S. National Park Service, "Turtles," Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A painted turtle resting on a sunny mossy log with a soft bird feather lying beside it.
image.caption: Feathers, the outer plates on most turtle shells and your fingernails are all built from tough proteins.

hops.title: Compare it: tree stump rings and the ridges on a fish scale
hops.text: Save this one for after the sort. A cut tree stump has one ring for each year the tree grew. Some fish keep a record like that on their scales: new ridges on a scale form closer together in winter, so scientists count those winter bands to guess how old the fish is.

sources.citation: U.S. National Park Service, "Dendrochronology: The Study of Tree Rings"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A slice of tree stump with rings beside a shimmering silver fish scale with faint ridges.
image.caption: Tree stumps and some fish scales both keep a record of the years they grew.
